title: The Decision Lab directory: operational annotation reference
scope: All entries linked in the specified biases directory; not all behavioral concepts anywhere on the website.
status: Reference ontology and synthetic teaching examples; not adjudicated training gold.
provenance: Source names and concept coverage from The Decision Lab; definitions are paraphrased and operationalized; examples and annotation policies are original. Source pages are references, not gold-standard empirical validation.

entries.name: AI Literacy Gap
entries.operational_definition: Comfort using AI exceeds understanding of its capabilities and limitations.
entries.positive_example: I use chatbots daily, so I am an AI expert; I did not know they can invent references.
entries.target_negative_example: I use chatbots daily but still need training in how to evaluate their answers.
entries.annotation_boundary: Require evidence of a competence gap; frequent use alone is insufficient.

entries.name: Accountability diffusion in AI
entries.operational_definition: Responsibility becomes dispersed across AI stakeholders until nobody accepts ownership.
entries.positive_example: The editor blamed the model, the vendor blamed the editor, and the deployment team said checking factual errors belonged to neither of them.
entries.target_negative_example: The editor reviews AI drafts and remains accountable for their accuracy.
entries.annotation_boundary: Distributed work alone is not diffusion; look for responsibility being disclaimed or left unowned.

entries.name: Action Bias
entries.operational_definition: Action is preferred simply to act, without a supporting advantage over waiting.
entries.positive_example: Monitoring is more likely to solve this temporary glitch, but change every setting now so we are doing something.
entries.target_negative_example: Restart the service because diagnostics show a restart will clear the fault.
entries.annotation_boundary: An evidence-based intervention is not action bias.

entries.name: Affect Heuristic
entries.operational_definition: An emotional reaction substitutes for evaluation of an option's benefits or risks.
entries.positive_example: The logo makes me feel peaceful, so the product must be safe; I have not checked its specifications.
entries.target_negative_example: I prefer this logo because I want a calming design.
entries.annotation_boundary: Emotion relevant to a subjective preference is not necessarily a distorted factual judgment.

entries.name: Ambiguity Effect
entries.operational_definition: Unspecified probabilities make an option less attractive than one with known probabilities.
entries.positive_example: I prefer the urn with a known 50% winning chance to the one with an unspecified mix, solely because its odds are known.
entries.target_negative_example: I prefer the first urn because a verified count gives it better odds.
entries.annotation_boundary: Ambiguity aversion can reflect a legitimate preference; do not equate it automatically with error.

entries.name: Anchoring Bias
entries.operational_definition: An initial value pulls a later estimate toward it despite weak relevance.
entries.positive_example: After seeing the randomly assigned number 800, I estimated 750 attendees; without it I had estimated 300.
entries.target_negative_example: I estimated 750 attendees from 750 confirmed registrations.
entries.annotation_boundary: Require an anchor affecting judgment, not merely the presence of a number.

entries.name: Attentional Bias
entries.operational_definition: Attention selectively favors certain information while other relevant information is overlooked.
entries.positive_example: When anxious, I notice every hesitation in the feedback meeting but miss the equally clear statements of approval.
entries.target_negative_example: I recorded both the criticisms and the praise before evaluating the feedback.
entries.annotation_boundary: Distinguish selective attention from a later judgment that weights negative evidence more heavily.

entries.name: Authority Bias
entries.operational_definition: Status or authority is treated as sufficient grounds for accepting a claim.
entries.positive_example: The celebrity historian says this bridge design is safe, so engineering calculations are unnecessary.
entries.target_negative_example: I accepted the structural engineer's conclusion after reviewing the supporting calculations.
entries.annotation_boundary: Appropriate reliance on relevant expertise is not enough to establish bias.

entries.name: Automation Bias
entries.operational_definition: Automated recommendations receive excessive trust despite reasons to check or reject them.
entries.positive_example: The spreadsheet total is visibly wrong, but the AI says it is correct, so I will approve it.
entries.target_negative_example: The AI suggested a total; I recalculated it before approval.
entries.annotation_boundary: Using automation alone is insufficient; identify unjustified deference.

entries.name: Availability Heuristic
entries.operational_definition: Ease of recalling examples substitutes for evidence about frequency or probability.
entries.positive_example: I can instantly recall three elevator accidents from videos, so elevators must fail frequently, regardless of the maintenance statistics.
entries.target_negative_example: The inspection database reports an increased failure rate, so I updated my estimate.
entries.annotation_boundary: Recency can make examples accessible, but the diagnostic mechanism is recall-based likelihood judgment.

entries.name: Bandwagon Effect
entries.operational_definition: A belief or choice gains appeal because many others adopt it.
entries.positive_example: I thought the proposal was weak, but everyone now supports it, so I support it too; no new evidence appeared.
entries.target_negative_example: I changed my mind after supporters supplied a successful pilot evaluation.
entries.annotation_boundary: Popularity must drive adoption; others can also provide useful evidence.

entries.name: Barnum Effect
entries.operational_definition: A vague description applicable to many people is accepted as uniquely personal.
entries.positive_example: This profile says I sometimes want company and sometimes solitude; it describes me so uniquely that it must know my personality.
entries.target_negative_example: The profile contains broad statements that fit many people, including me.
entries.annotation_boundary: Agreement with a general statement alone is insufficient; require perceived personal specificity.

entries.name: Base Rate Fallacy
entries.operational_definition: Relevant population prevalence is neglected in favor of case-specific information.
entries.positive_example: Only 1% of these messages are scams. The detector catches all scams but flags 10% of legitimate messages. A flagged message is therefore almost certainly a scam.
entries.target_negative_example: A flag is worth investigating, but false alarms may outnumber real scams because scams are rare.
entries.annotation_boundary: Require an available relevant base rate being neglected; overlap with representativeness is possible.

entries.name: Belief Perseverance (The Backfire Effect)
entries.operational_definition: A belief persists after its supporting evidence is discredited; strengthening after correction is a distinct backfire pattern.
entries.positive_example: The photo was my only evidence. Even after its creator proved it was staged, I still believe it depicts the event.
entries.target_negative_example: The photo was staged, so I withdraw the claim it supported.
entries.annotation_boundary: Preserved source umbrella: record perseverance and backfire as separate subtypes; persistence does not imply strengthening.

entries.name: Benjamin Franklin effect
entries.operational_definition: Doing someone a favor leads the helper to like that person more.
entries.positive_example: I disliked Omar, but after voluntarily helping him move, I found myself liking him more even though I learned nothing new about him.
entries.target_negative_example: I liked Omar more after discovering that he had quietly helped my family.
entries.annotation_boundary: The direction is giving a favor then increased liking, not receiving kindness then liking its giver.

entries.name: Bikeshedding
entries.operational_definition: Disproportionate discussion goes to easy trivial details while consequential issues receive little scrutiny.
entries.positive_example: We approved the unexamined infrastructure plan in five minutes, then spent two hours debating the slide colors.
entries.target_negative_example: We spent two hours resolving a safety-critical control setting.
entries.annotation_boundary: Judge time against importance; a small-looking detail can have major consequences.

entries.name: Bottom-Dollar Effect
entries.operational_definition: Spending the last available funds reduces satisfaction with the purchased item.
entries.positive_example: The meal was identical, but buying it with my last discretionary money made it feel less satisfying than when I had money left.
entries.target_negative_example: The meal disappointed me because it arrived cold.
entries.annotation_boundary: Distinguish diminished purchase satisfaction from rational concern about an insufficient budget.

entries.name: Bounded Rationality
entries.operational_definition: Limited time, information, or processing capacity leads to a satisfactory rather than globally optimal choice.
entries.positive_example: I had ten minutes to find a room, so I booked the first one meeting my price and location requirements.
entries.target_negative_example: I compared every available room against a fully specified criterion and selected the highest-scoring one.
entries.annotation_boundary: A decision framework, not inherently an error; label satisficing only when constraints and stopping rule are visible.

entries.name: Bundling Bias
entries.operational_definition: Bundled pricing weakens attention to the cost of individual components and can reduce their use.
entries.positive_example: I would attend each separately paid workshop, but the same workshops in a package feel already absorbed into one price, so I skip several.
entries.target_negative_example: I skipped the workshops because they were cancelled.
entries.annotation_boundary: Underuse must relate to bundling; a bundle purchase alone proves nothing.

entries.name: Bye-Now Effect
entries.operational_definition: Exposure to the word bye is proposed to activate buy through their shared sound and influence spending.
entries.positive_example: In this hypothetical randomized study, shoppers shown 'bye' subsequently spent more than the matched neutral-word group, with all offers unchanged.
entries.target_negative_example: The cashier said 'bye' after I completed my planned purchase.
entries.annotation_boundary: A narrow proposed priming effect; an isolated word or purchase cannot establish the mechanism.

entries.name: Cashless Effect
entries.operational_definition: Cash-free payment increases willingness to spend relative to physical cash.
entries.positive_example: With the same budget and price, I reject the purchase when paying in notes but accept it by tapping my card because the payment feels less real.
entries.target_negative_example: I use a card to purchase the same planned item at the same price.
entries.annotation_boundary: Require a change in spending or willingness, not just card usage.

entries.name: Category Size Bias
entries.operational_definition: A particular outcome is judged more likely because it belongs to a larger category, although individual outcome probabilities are equal.
entries.positive_example: A fair draw selects one of ten equally likely tokens. Eight are blue and two are red. I say the specific token Blue-1 is more likely than Red-1 solely because blue is the larger group.
entries.target_negative_example: Blue-1 and Red-1 each have a 10% chance; the blue category as a whole has an 80% chance.
entries.annotation_boundary: Distinguish an individual outcome from its category; larger categories can genuinely have greater aggregate probability.

entries.name: Choice Overload
entries.operational_definition: A larger choice set impairs choosing or satisfaction through comparison difficulty.
entries.positive_example: With six suitable lamps I chose easily; with sixty similarly suitable lamps I became overwhelmed and abandoned the purchase.
entries.target_negative_example: I rejected all sixty lamps because none fit the required socket.
entries.annotation_boundary: Many options alone are insufficient; identify overload and its consequence.

entries.name: Cognitive Dissonance
entries.operational_definition: Inconsistent beliefs, values, or behavior produce discomfort and efforts to resolve the inconsistency.
entries.positive_example: I value equal treatment but favor my friends at work. That contradiction bothers me, so I tell myself fairness does not matter here.
entries.target_negative_example: I noticed that I had two inconsistent estimates and checked which calculation was wrong.
entries.annotation_boundary: Dissonance is a psychological state; resolution through honest revision is not itself biased reasoning.

entries.name: Commitment Bias
entries.operational_definition: A prior commitment is maintained or escalated despite evidence that it should be reconsidered.
entries.positive_example: I publicly backed this process, so we must keep it even though the trial shows it fails and switching has no additional cost.
entries.target_negative_example: We will keep the process because the new trial demonstrates it works better.
entries.annotation_boundary: Public consistency can distinguish commitment bias from a specific appeal to unrecoverable expenditure.

entries.name: Confirmation Bias
entries.operational_definition: Evidence is sought, interpreted, or accepted selectively to support an existing belief.
entries.positive_example: I believe remote work fails, so include the negative studies and omit the equally rigorous positive ones.
entries.target_negative_example: Include studies both for and against remote work using the same quality criteria.
entries.annotation_boundary: Disagreement alone is not confirmation bias; identify asymmetric treatment of evidence.

entries.name: Decision Fatigue
entries.operational_definition: Repeated decision-making is followed by mental exhaustion and poorer or more avoidant choices.
entries.positive_example: After choosing among suppliers all day, I felt too drained to compare the final bids and accepted the default without reading them.
entries.target_negative_example: I accepted the default after checking that it offered the best terms.
entries.annotation_boundary: Require the decision-load link; time of day alone cannot establish fatigue or its cause.

entries.name: Declinism
entries.operational_definition: The past is idealized while the present or future is judged to be deteriorating without adequate support.
entries.positive_example: Everything in society keeps getting worse; I dismiss the long-term improvements because the past must have been better.
entries.target_negative_example: This specific service has deteriorated according to a consistent ten-year performance series.
entries.annotation_boundary: A supported decline in one measure is not generalized declinism.

entries.name: Decoy Effect
entries.operational_definition: An asymmetrically dominated third option shifts preference toward the option that dominates it.
entries.positive_example: I preferred the €6 small plan to the €10 large plan. Adding a €10 medium plan with fewer benefits than the large made me choose the large, although the original plans stayed unchanged.
entries.target_negative_example: I chose the large plan after its price fell below the small plan's price.
entries.annotation_boundary: Show the third option's dominance relation and a preference shift.

entries.name: Delegation Creep
entries.operational_definition: AI delegation expands gradually into new or consequential tasks without a corresponding review of suitability.
entries.positive_example: The tool first sorted notes, then drafted recommendations, and now decides which projects to cancel; nobody assessed its new role.
entries.target_negative_example: Before expanding the tool's role, we validated the new use and assigned review responsibility.
entries.annotation_boundary: A temporal expansion is essential; one instance of automated advice is not creep.

entries.name: Disposition Effect
entries.operational_definition: Losing investments are retained and winning ones sold because of their gain-loss status rather than forward prospects.
entries.positive_example: I sell anything above my purchase price and keep anything below it until it breaks even, regardless of updated prospects.
entries.target_negative_example: I sell the asset whose future outlook worsened, even though it has gained since purchase.
entries.annotation_boundary: Purchase price alone should not substitute for forward evaluation; taxes and strategy can justify trades.

entries.name: Distinction Bias
entries.operational_definition: Side-by-side comparison exaggerates differences that matter little during separate use.
entries.positive_example: Comparing the screens together, I predict a tiny color difference will dominate my enjoyment; using each alone, I cannot notice it.
entries.target_negative_example: I compare two monitors because my work requires side-by-side color matching.
entries.annotation_boundary: Joint versus separate evaluation matters; a real use-relevant difference is not sufficient evidence of bias.

entries.name: Dunning–Kruger Effect
entries.operational_definition: Low demonstrated competence accompanies overestimation of competence and difficulty recognizing errors.
entries.positive_example: I scored 2 out of 20 on repeated calibration tasks but insist I am among the best and cannot identify my basic mistakes even when asked to review them.
entries.target_negative_example: I am new to this subject and expect to make mistakes.
entries.annotation_boundary: Do not diagnose from confidence or disagreement alone; a single anecdote cannot establish a population-level effect.

entries.name: Einstellung Effect
entries.operational_definition: A familiar solution blocks discovery of a better alternative.
entries.positive_example: I kept applying the old ten-step procedure and failed to notice the new two-step solution because I assumed the old method was the only route.
entries.target_negative_example: I chose the familiar procedure after testing and ruling out the shorter route.
entries.annotation_boundary: Focus on fixation on a learned solution, rather than a general preference for a familiar tool.

entries.name: Empathy Gap
entries.operational_definition: A person underestimates how a different emotional or bodily state changes preferences and behavior.
entries.positive_example: While comfortably full, I insist being hungry would never alter my patience, despite repeatedly becoming irritable when hungry.
entries.target_negative_example: I schedule a break because I know hunger may affect my patience.
entries.annotation_boundary: Require a mismatch across states or failure to understand another person's state.

entries.name: Endowment Effect
entries.operational_definition: Ownership raises valuation beyond the value assigned before owning the same item.
entries.positive_example: I would pay €20 for this identical mug, but once it became mine I demanded €60 solely because it was mine.
entries.target_negative_example: I ask €60 because this mug has documented features absent from the €20 version.
entries.annotation_boundary: Ownership must explain the valuation gap; market differences and transaction costs may explain it instead.

entries.name: Extrinsic Incentive Bias
entries.operational_definition: Others' motivation is attributed more to external rewards than one's own motivation is.
entries.positive_example: I work for the intellectual challenge, but my equally enthusiastic colleagues must only care about bonuses; I have no evidence of that difference.
entries.target_negative_example: My colleague told me she accepted this assignment specifically for its bonus.
entries.annotation_boundary: Require an unsupported self-other asymmetry, not any mention of money.

entries.name: False Consensus Effect
entries.operational_definition: Agreement with one's own position is overestimated.
entries.positive_example: I dislike open offices, so I estimate almost everyone dislikes them, although the representative survey shows an even split.
entries.target_negative_example: I dislike open offices but know the survey shows divided preferences.
entries.annotation_boundary: Different from pluralistic ignorance, which involves a mistaken belief that one's private view is not shared.

entries.name: Framing Effect
entries.operational_definition: Equivalent information yields different choices when expressed differently.
entries.positive_example: I reject the service labeled '10% unsuccessful' but accept the identical service labeled '90% successful.'
entries.target_negative_example: I choose the service with a verified 95% success rate over one with 90%.
entries.annotation_boundary: Check mathematical and substantive equivalence; genuinely different information is not framing alone.

entries.name: Functional Fixedness
entries.operational_definition: An object's customary purpose blocks recognition of another useful purpose.
entries.positive_example: We need a temporary weight, but I overlook the heavy book because I think books can only be used for reading.
entries.target_negative_example: I avoid using the book as a weight because it would damage a fragile surface.
entries.annotation_boundary: Object-use restriction differs from fixation on an established problem-solving procedure.

entries.name: Fundamental Attribution Error
entries.operational_definition: Behavior is attributed too strongly to character while relevant situational constraints are discounted.
entries.positive_example: Her call dropped during a documented network outage; that proves she is inconsiderate, whatever the outage did.
entries.target_negative_example: The outage explains the dropped call; it tells me little about her character.
entries.annotation_boundary: A character judgment needs evidence of neglected context to support this label confidently.

entries.name: Gambler's Fallacy
entries.operational_definition: Independent random outcomes are expected to reverse because of previous outcomes.
entries.positive_example: This fair coin produced five heads, so tails is now more likely on the next independent toss.
entries.target_negative_example: The next toss still has a 50% chance of tails.
entries.annotation_boundary: Require independence or stable probabilities; sampling without replacement can change the odds.

entries.name: Google Effect
entries.operational_definition: Expected access to external information reduces memory for the information itself.
entries.positive_example: When told I could reopen the saved lookup, I remembered where it was but retained less of its content than when told it would disappear.
entries.target_negative_example: I used a search engine and then accurately recalled the information.
entries.annotation_boundary: External lookup alone is insufficient; this is a memory/offloading effect, not automatically faulty reasoning.

entries.name: Halo Effect
entries.operational_definition: A favorable impression on one dimension spills into an unsupported judgment on another.
entries.positive_example: The applicant is stylish, so she must also be excellent at debugging; I have not assessed that skill.
entries.target_negative_example: The applicant solved our debugging exercise accurately, so I rated that skill highly.
entries.annotation_boundary: Require cross-attribute spillover; competence inferred from relevant performance is different.

entries.name: Hard-easy effect
entries.operational_definition: Confidence tends to be too high for difficult tasks and too low for easy tasks.
entries.positive_example: Across a scored test, my difficult-item confidence averaged 80% with 30% accuracy, while easy-item confidence averaged 70% with 95% accuracy.
entries.target_negative_example: My confidence approximately matched my accuracy in both difficulty groups.
entries.annotation_boundary: This is a calibration pattern across difficulty levels, not simply being overconfident once.

entries.name: Heuristics
entries.operational_definition: A simplified rule reduces the information or computation used to decide.
entries.positive_example: When short of time, I use a rough rule to select a route rather than calculating every alternative.
entries.target_negative_example: I exhaustively evaluated all routes using the specified objective.
entries.annotation_boundary: Umbrella concept; prefer a named subtype when supported, and do not assume a shortcut is inaccurate.

entries.name: Hindsight Bias
entries.operational_definition: Knowing the outcome makes it seem more predictable beforehand than it was.
entries.positive_example: I said the match was impossible to call. After the result, I insist I knew the winner all along.
entries.target_negative_example: My dated pre-match prediction named the winner and expressed the same confidence I report now.
entries.annotation_boundary: Different from judging the quality of the original decision by its outcome.

entries.name: Hot Hand Fallacy
entries.operational_definition: A success streak is treated as evidence of increased next-trial success without support.
entries.positive_example: The independent random generator gave me three wins, so I am on a streak and my next win is more likely.
entries.target_negative_example: The generator's independent win probability remains unchanged.
entries.annotation_boundary: Real persistence can exist in skill-based activities; do not label every streak inference a fallacy.

entries.name: Hyperbolic Discounting
entries.operational_definition: Impatience decreases with delay, producing preferences consistent with non-exponential discounting.
entries.positive_example: I choose €40 today over €50 tomorrow, but choose €50 in 31 days over €40 in 30 days under otherwise identical conditions.
entries.target_negative_example: I use the same proportional discount rate for equivalent intervals at all delays.
entries.annotation_boundary: This reversal supports decreasing impatience but does not prove an exact hyperbolic function; it overlaps present bias.

entries.name: IKEA Effect
entries.operational_definition: Personal assembly or creation inflates an object's perceived value.
entries.positive_example: I rank my self-assembled shelf above an indistinguishable ready-made one solely because I built it.
entries.target_negative_example: My shelf is more valuable to me because its custom dimensions fit my room.
entries.annotation_boundary: Separate construction effort from ownership alone and from objective customization benefits.

entries.name: Identifiable Victim Effect
entries.operational_definition: An identified individual elicits more help than comparable anonymous beneficiaries.
entries.positive_example: I donate more when shown one named beneficiary than when the identical need is presented anonymously, with effectiveness held constant.
entries.target_negative_example: I choose the program with verified greater benefit per donation.
entries.annotation_boundary: Identification must drive the difference; differing effectiveness can justify allocation.

entries.name: Illusion of Control
entries.operational_definition: Personal actions are believed to control outcomes they cannot influence.
entries.positive_example: Pressing the lottery button with my lucky finger makes this independent random draw more likely to win.
entries.target_negative_example: Pressing the button starts the draw but does not change its odds.
entries.annotation_boundary: Actual causal influence is not illusory control.

entries.name: Illusion of Transparency
entries.operational_definition: Internal feelings or intentions are assumed to be more visible to others than they are.
entries.positive_example: Although observers could not tell I was nervous, I was certain they could read every anxious thought from my neutral expression.
entries.target_negative_example: I told the audience I was nervous, so they knew.
entries.annotation_boundary: Internal-state visibility differs from believing one receives unusually much attention.

entries.name: Illusion of Validity
entries.operational_definition: A coherent impression creates unwarranted confidence in the validity of a prediction.
entries.positive_example: These unvalidated interview impressions form such a consistent story that I am certain they predict performance, despite near-chance results in past tests.
entries.target_negative_example: I report uncertainty because the interview method lacks predictive validation.
entries.annotation_boundary: Focus on confidence in an unreliable inference, not confidence alone.

entries.name: Illusory Correlation
entries.operational_definition: A relationship is perceived despite insufficient evidence or contrary association data.
entries.positive_example: I believe rainy days cause software failures because the pair stands out in memory, although the logs show equal failure rates on wet and dry days.
entries.target_negative_example: The logs show an association; further work is needed to assess causation.
entries.annotation_boundary: Distinguish an unsupported association from the separate mistake of treating a real correlation as causation.

entries.name: Illusory Truth Effect
entries.operational_definition: Repeated exposure makes a claim seem truer without new supporting evidence.
entries.positive_example: The rumor sounded doubtful initially, but after seeing the same unsourced sentence twenty times I now think it is true.
entries.target_negative_example: I believed the claim after independent records verified it.
entries.annotation_boundary: Repeated independent evidence differs from repetition of the same unsupported claim.

entries.name: Impact Bias
entries.operational_definition: The intensity or duration of future emotional reactions is overestimated.
entries.positive_example: I predicted losing the contest would make every day miserable for a year; a month later I had largely adjusted.
entries.target_negative_example: I expect disappointment but do not know how intense or lasting it will be.
entries.annotation_boundary: An emotional forecast needs a basis for judging overestimation; intense feelings alone are not bias.

entries.name: In-group Bias
entries.operational_definition: Shared group membership leads to preferential evaluation or treatment.
entries.positive_example: The candidates performed equally, but I rated the one from my own club higher solely because she is one of us.
entries.target_negative_example: I selected the candidate with stronger relevant performance regardless of club.
entries.annotation_boundary: Group membership must drive unequal treatment; relevant qualifications are an alternative explanation.

entries.name: Incentivization
entries.operational_definition: Rewards or penalties alter motivation or behavior.
entries.positive_example: When each completed practice set earned a token, participants completed more sets than in the otherwise identical no-token condition.
entries.target_negative_example: Practice increased before any reward was introduced, with no change after it.
entries.annotation_boundary: A motivational mechanism, not inherently a cognitive bias or evidence of manipulation.

entries.name: Just-world Hypothesis
entries.operational_definition: People's outcomes are assumed to reflect what they morally deserve.
entries.positive_example: She was cheated, so she must have done something to deserve it; innocent people would not suffer that outcome.
entries.target_negative_example: The evidence shows she was deceived; suffering does not establish wrongdoing.
entries.annotation_boundary: Do not infer this label from a supported claim about consequences of a specific action.

entries.name: Lag Effect
entries.operational_definition: Within spaced practice, longer suitable intervals can improve later retention relative to shorter intervals.
entries.positive_example: With equal study time and a fixed later test, the group with longer review gaps remembered more than the short-gap group.
entries.target_negative_example: The groups had identical gaps but different total study time.
entries.annotation_boundary: Intervals have limits and depend on the retention horizon; longer is not universally better.

entries.name: Law of the Instrument
entries.operational_definition: A familiar tool or skill is applied too broadly even when poorly suited.
entries.positive_example: Since learning regression, I insist every problem must be solved with regression, including tasks that require a simple document lookup.
entries.target_negative_example: I chose regression after checking that its assumptions and purpose fit the problem.
entries.annotation_boundary: Tool overgeneralization differs from an object's fixed customary use.

entries.name: Less-is-Better Effect
entries.operational_definition: Separate evaluation favors a smaller or objectively lesser option, while joint evaluation reverses the preference.
entries.positive_example: Rated alone, eight pristine glasses score above ten identical pristine glasses plus two chipped extras; viewed together, the larger set wins even though the extras are freely discardable.
entries.target_negative_example: I choose eight glasses because storage is limited and unwanted extras cannot be discarded.
entries.annotation_boundary: Show the evaluation context and control genuine costs of the extra items.

entries.name: Leveling and Sharpening
entries.operational_definition: Retelling flattens some details and accentuates others, distorting the remembered account.
entries.positive_example: The recording showed a mixed discussion; after several retellings, I omitted every qualification and remembered a mild objection as a furious confrontation.
entries.target_negative_example: I shortened the account while preserving its meaning and marking omitted details.
entries.annotation_boundary: Ordinary summarization is not necessarily memory distortion; intentional editing needs separate attribution.

entries.name: Levels of Processing
entries.operational_definition: Meaning-focused processing supports better memory than shallow surface processing.
entries.positive_example: After equal exposure, I recalled words I related to personal experiences better than words whose font I inspected.
entries.target_negative_example: I remembered one list better because I studied it three times longer.
entries.annotation_boundary: A memory framework, not an irrational judgment; compare processing depth with exposure controlled.

entries.name: Look-elsewhere Effect
entries.operational_definition: Searching many tests or locations increases the chance of apparently impressive findings, which can be overstated if multiplicity is ignored.
entries.positive_example: We tested 200 unrelated comparisons and advertised the one with p below .05 as decisive, without correcting for the search.
entries.target_negative_example: We disclosed all comparisons and assessed significance with multiplicity accounted for.
entries.annotation_boundary: The statistical effect need not involve dishonesty; distinguish exploratory discovery from confirmatory evidence.

entries.name: Loss Aversion
entries.operational_definition: A loss relative to a reference point carries more psychological weight than an equal gain.
entries.positive_example: In matched choices, losing ten tokens hurts me much more than gaining ten pleases me.
entries.target_negative_example: I avoid this gamble because I cannot afford the possible loss.
entries.annotation_boundary: Risk aversion or inability to absorb a loss alone does not establish loss aversion.

entries.name: Mental Accounting
entries.operational_definition: Money is treated differently according to mental categories rather than its interchangeable purchasing power.
entries.positive_example: I will spend the unexpected €100 prize frivolously but would never spend €100 of salary that way, despite identical needs and finances.
entries.target_negative_example: I keep a rent budget to ensure I can meet a fixed upcoming payment.
entries.annotation_boundary: Budgeting can be useful; identify a category-driven inconsistency before calling it erroneous.

entries.name: Mere Exposure Effect
entries.operational_definition: Repeated exposure increases liking without new substantive information.
entries.positive_example: After repeatedly seeing the same abstract pattern, I liked it more than an equally novel pattern I had seen only once.
entries.target_negative_example: I liked the design more after learning it was easier to read.
entries.annotation_boundary: Liking through familiarity differs from believing a repeated claim is true.

entries.name: Messenger Effect
entries.operational_definition: The identity or presentation of a messenger changes reception of an otherwise identical message.
entries.positive_example: I dismiss this identical safety statement when read by an unfamiliar person but accept it from a charming presenter with no additional expertise.
entries.target_negative_example: I give more weight to a source with directly relevant, independently verified expertise.
entries.annotation_boundary: Messenger cues can be informative; authority bias is a more specific subtype when status drives deference.

entries.name: Motivating Uncertainty Effect
entries.operational_definition: Uncertainty about a reward's size can increase effort through excitement about pursuing it.
entries.positive_example: I worked harder for a mystery token prize than a certain prize of equal expected value because discovering the prize made the task exciting.
entries.target_negative_example: I worked harder for the mystery prize because its expected value was much higher.
entries.annotation_boundary: Control reward value and focus on pursuit; uncertainty is not universally motivating.

entries.name: Naive Allocation
entries.operational_definition: Resources are spread evenly across listed options without considering their underlying differences.
entries.positive_example: I put one quarter in each of four funds solely because there are four, ignoring that three hold the same assets.
entries.target_negative_example: I chose equal weights after assessing exposures and finding they fit my objective.
entries.annotation_boundary: Equal allocation is not automatically naive; require the superficial allocation rule.

entries.name: Naive Realism
entries.operational_definition: One's own perspective is treated as unmediated reality and disagreement as others' defect.
entries.positive_example: I simply see the facts objectively; anyone who interprets this ambiguous scene differently must be ignorant or biased.
entries.target_negative_example: We may weigh the same evidence differently; let us compare assumptions.
entries.annotation_boundary: Believing a well-supported fact does not itself demonstrate naive realism.

entries.name: Negativity Bias
entries.operational_definition: Negative information receives disproportionate weight relative to comparable positive information.
entries.positive_example: Nine equally credible compliments and one mild criticism arrived; I treated the criticism as defining the entire evaluation.
entries.target_negative_example: One criticism exposed a serious safety defect, outweighing nine compliments about appearance.
entries.annotation_boundary: Severity and relevance can justify unequal weights; count alone is not enough.

entries.name: Noble Edge Effect
entries.operational_definition: Perceived corporate social responsibility increases favorable evaluation or purchase appeal.
entries.positive_example: Learning that the brand genuinely funds a community library increased my respect and willingness to buy its otherwise unchanged headphones.
entries.target_negative_example: Learning about the donation did not change my evaluation or willingness to buy.
entries.annotation_boundary: A favorable ethical preference is not automatically irrational; an unsupported leap to better sound quality would also suggest halo effect.

entries.name: Normalcy Bias
entries.operational_definition: Continuation of ordinary conditions is assumed despite credible signs of disruption.
entries.positive_example: The warning system confirms an imminent disruption, but it cannot happen here because our routine has always continued before.
entries.target_negative_example: I checked the warning and found it referred to a different location.
entries.annotation_boundary: Require neglect of credible warning evidence, not simply remaining calm.

entries.name: Nostalgia Effect
entries.operational_definition: Nostalgic feelings increase willingness to spend or weaken attachment to money.
entries.positive_example: Remembering childhood gatherings made me more willing to spend on the same reunion purchase than when I felt neutral.
entries.target_negative_example: I remember childhood fondly but keep the same purchase decision.
entries.annotation_boundary: Nostalgia alone is insufficient for this source's spending-related effect.

entries.name: Observer Expectancy Effect
entries.operational_definition: An observer's expectations influence the people being observed, potentially contaminating results.
entries.positive_example: Expecting one group to cooperate, the facilitator unconsciously gave it warmer encouragement; participants responded by cooperating more.
entries.target_negative_example: The blinded facilitator used the same script and encouragement for all groups.
entries.annotation_boundary: Require an expectation-mediated influence; merely knowing one is watched is not enough. Expectation-biased scoring is a related measurement mechanism.

entries.name: Omission Bias
entries.operational_definition: Harm caused by acting is judged more harshly than comparable harm caused by not acting.
entries.positive_example: With knowledge, responsibility, and consequences held equal, I judge deliberately withholding the warning less wrong than deliberately disabling it solely because withholding is doing nothing.
entries.target_negative_example: I judge the cases differently because only one person knew the warning was necessary.
entries.annotation_boundary: Control knowledge, duty, intention, and consequences before attributing an action-inaction asymmetry.

entries.name: Optimism Bias
entries.operational_definition: Positive outcomes are expected too strongly or negative outcomes discounted without adequate grounds.
entries.positive_example: Comparable teams succeed 30% of the time; we have no distinguishing advantage, but I am certain we will succeed because we are us.
entries.target_negative_example: Our estimate is higher because validated evidence shows our process differs materially.
entries.annotation_boundary: Hope and supported favorable forecasts are not enough to establish bias.

entries.name: Ostrich Effect
entries.operational_definition: Threatening information is avoided to escape discomfort.
entries.positive_example: I suspect the project is over budget, but I refuse to open the report because seeing the bad news would upset me.
entries.target_negative_example: I will review the report tomorrow when the corrected data arrive.
entries.annotation_boundary: Information avoidance differs from believing no threat exists; a practical delay may be justified.

entries.name: Outcome bias
entries.operational_definition: A decision is evaluated by its result instead of the reasoning and evidence available when it was made.
entries.positive_example: The unsupported guess happened to be right, so guessing without evidence was an excellent decision.
entries.target_negative_example: The guess was poorly supported even though luck made it right.
entries.annotation_boundary: Outcome bias concerns decision quality; hindsight bias concerns prior predictability.

entries.name: Overjustification Effect
entries.operational_definition: External rewards reduce previously intrinsic interest in an activity.
entries.positive_example: I used to draw for enjoyment; after being paid per picture, I lost interest in unpaid drawing even though I still had the time and materials.
entries.target_negative_example: I draw less because my new job leaves no free time.
entries.annotation_boundary: Require prior intrinsic interest and a reward-related decline, not any decrease in activity.

entries.name: Parasocial Trust in AI
entries.operational_definition: A humanlike AI relationship creates trust, disclosure, or deference unsupported by its actual capabilities.
entries.positive_example: The chatbot remembers my favorite songs and feels like a loyal friend, so I trust its unverified advice about every major decision.
entries.target_negative_example: I enjoy its warm tone but evaluate its claims independently.
entries.annotation_boundary: Warm interaction alone is insufficient; identify relational trust driving reliance or disclosure.

entries.name: Peak-end Rule
entries.operational_definition: Retrospective evaluation disproportionately reflects the most intense moment and the ending.
entries.positive_example: I called the mostly tedious workshop excellent because one demonstration was thrilling and the final minute was delightful, disregarding the rest.
entries.target_negative_example: I rated the workshop by considering the full session, including duration and typical experience.
entries.annotation_boundary: A mentioned ending alone is insufficient; identify disproportionate retrospective weighting.

entries.name: Pessimism bias
entries.operational_definition: Negative outcomes are expected too strongly and favorable outcomes discounted without adequate support.
entries.positive_example: The reliable test suggests a 90% chance of success, but without contrary evidence I am sure it will fail.
entries.target_negative_example: The test shows a 10% chance of success, so failure is more likely.
entries.annotation_boundary: Distinguish unsupported pessimism from a justified adverse forecast.

entries.name: Planning Fallacy
entries.operational_definition: Completion time or resources are underestimated despite relevant experience and constraints.
entries.positive_example: Every comparable edit took two weeks; with unchanged resources and scope, I budget two days because I imagine everything going smoothly.
entries.target_negative_example: I use the two-week reference-class estimate and add time for the new requirement.
entries.annotation_boundary: A short estimate is not enough; require neglected evidence or demonstrated underestimation.

entries.name: Pluralistic Ignorance
entries.operational_definition: People mistakenly believe their privately held view differs from the group's view and conform to that misperception.
entries.positive_example: Everyone privately dislikes the ritual, but each thinks everyone else likes it, so all continue participating.
entries.target_negative_example: Most participants genuinely like the ritual, and I know I am in the minority.
entries.annotation_boundary: Ground truth about private group views distinguishes shared misperception from actual disagreement.

entries.name: Present Bias
entries.operational_definition: Immediate outcomes receive disproportionate weight relative to otherwise comparable delayed outcomes.
entries.positive_example: Yesterday I chose tomorrow's larger reward over today's smaller one; now that the smaller one is immediately available, I reverse my choice without any change in need.
entries.target_negative_example: I take the smaller payment now because I must meet an unavoidable payment today.
entries.annotation_boundary: Liquidity and changing circumstances can justify immediacy; overlap with decreasing-impatience models.

entries.name: Primacy Effect
entries.operational_definition: Early items in a sequence are remembered better or disproportionately shape impressions.
entries.positive_example: With equally distinctive words and equal exposure, I recall the first few much better than those in the middle.
entries.target_negative_example: I remember the first word because it was repeated ten extra times.
entries.annotation_boundary: Control distinctiveness and exposure; this is a component of serial position effects.

entries.name: Priming
entries.operational_definition: Earlier exposure changes later processing or responses without a deliberate inferential link.
entries.positive_example: After a brief exposure to bread-related words, I recognized 'butter' faster than after unrelated words in the matched task.
entries.target_negative_example: I selected butter after deliberately reading the recipe's ingredient list.
entries.annotation_boundary: Priming has multiple forms; word co-occurrence in a document cannot establish a priming effect.

entries.name: Projection Bias
entries.operational_definition: Current tastes or states are projected too strongly onto future preferences.
entries.positive_example: While very hungry, I order next week's portions assuming I will want exactly this much at every meal, though my appetite reliably falls when full.
entries.target_negative_example: I base next week's portions on my recorded appetite across normal meals.
entries.annotation_boundary: Related to empathy gap, but specifically concerns overprojecting present preferences onto the future.

entries.name: Reactive devaluation
entries.operational_definition: A proposal loses value because it comes from an adversary or disliked source.
entries.positive_example: I accepted these exact terms from the mediator, but reject them once told my rival proposed them, with every term unchanged.
entries.target_negative_example: I reject the revised proposal because its delivery deadline changed.
entries.annotation_boundary: Require source-driven devaluation; substantive differences or credible strategic risks can justify rejection.

entries.name: Recency Effect
entries.operational_definition: Recent items in a sequence receive a memory advantage or excessive judgmental weight.
entries.positive_example: After an equally presented list, I recall the final items better than the middle items.
entries.target_negative_example: I recall the final item because it was unusually vivid and repeated.
entries.annotation_boundary: A recent anecdote used to infer prevalence may instead involve availability; specify the mechanism.

entries.name: Regret Aversion
entries.operational_definition: Anticipated regret disproportionately discourages a choice.
entries.positive_example: Both options fit my goals, but I reject switching solely to avoid imagining how much I would blame myself if it later went badly.
entries.target_negative_example: I reject switching because the documented transition cost exceeds its benefit.
entries.annotation_boundary: Regret can be a real preference; establish disproportion or inconsistency before calling the choice irrational.

entries.name: Representativeness Heuristic
entries.operational_definition: Similarity to a prototype substitutes for probabilistic or categorical evidence.
entries.positive_example: She resembles my image of a poet, so she is probably a poet; I ignore how common other occupations are and have no work-history evidence.
entries.target_negative_example: Her published portfolio confirms that she works as a poet.
entries.annotation_boundary: Prototype reasoning can overlap base-rate neglect, but neither label automatically entails the other.

entries.name: Response Bias
entries.operational_definition: Survey or elicited responses are systematically distorted by response tendencies or the questioning situation.
entries.positive_example: With my supervisor watching, I report complete satisfaction even though I privately feel dissatisfied, because I want to appear cooperative.
entries.target_negative_example: I report satisfaction that matches my private assessment.
entries.annotation_boundary: An unusual answer or deliberate privacy choice alone does not establish a general response tendency; distinguish sampling bias.

entries.name: Restraint Bias
entries.operational_definition: The ability to resist temptation is overestimated.
entries.positive_example: I repeatedly exceed my gaming limit, but I am sure I can keep the game open all day and resist it without any change in strategy.
entries.target_negative_example: I close the game during work because I know temptation is difficult for me.
entries.annotation_boundary: Require self-control overconfidence rather than a single indulgence or general optimism.

entries.name: Rosy Retrospection
entries.operational_definition: Past experiences are recalled more positively than they were experienced.
entries.positive_example: My contemporaneous diary describes a miserable trip, but years later I remember it as almost entirely wonderful and forget the persistent difficulties.
entries.target_negative_example: My diary and present memory both describe the trip as enjoyable with a few problems.
entries.annotation_boundary: Positive remembrance alone is insufficient; distinguish nostalgic spending and broad societal declinism.

entries.name: Salience Bias
entries.operational_definition: Conspicuous information dominates attention or judgment beyond its relevance.
entries.positive_example: The flashing 'new' badge draws all my attention, so I ignore the plainly available performance table when choosing equipment.
entries.target_negative_example: I prioritize the bright warning because it identifies the most serious hazard.
entries.annotation_boundary: Salience concerns prominence; attentional bias is broader and can arise from internal concerns.

entries.name: Self-serving Bias
entries.operational_definition: Success is credited internally while failure is attributed externally in a self-favoring way.
entries.positive_example: When our unchanged process wins, it proves my skill; when it loses, it is entirely bad luck, without any evidence supporting that asymmetry.
entries.target_negative_example: I examine both my contribution and external conditions after wins and losses.
entries.annotation_boundary: Supported causal attributions are not biased merely because they reflect well on the speaker.

entries.name: Serial Position Effect
entries.operational_definition: Recall varies with list position, often favoring the beginning and end over the middle.
entries.positive_example: After equal presentation, I remember the first and last few items but very few middle items.
entries.target_negative_example: I recall items evenly across list positions.
entries.annotation_boundary: Primacy and recency are components; avoid counting the umbrella as an additional independent finding by default.

entries.name: Sexual Overperception Bias
entries.operational_definition: Another person's sexual interest is inferred beyond what the evidence supports.
entries.positive_example: Despite being told the interaction was only routine politeness, I insist the ordinary smile proves sexual interest.
entries.target_negative_example: The person explicitly expressed sexual interest, and I take that statement at face value.
entries.annotation_boundary: Do not infer from gender or friendliness alone; ambiguous interaction often warrants insufficient evidence.

entries.name: Social Norms
entries.operational_definition: Perceived shared practices or expectations influence behavior.
entries.positive_example: I lower my voice here because everyone treats quiet conversation as the expected behavior.
entries.target_negative_example: I lower my voice because my throat hurts.
entries.annotation_boundary: A social coordination mechanism, not inherently a bias; distinguish actual norms from misperceived norms.

entries.name: Source Confusion
entries.operational_definition: The origin of remembered information is forgotten or attributed to the wrong source.
entries.positive_example: I insist I witnessed the incident, but the records show I only heard someone describe it afterward.
entries.target_negative_example: I accurately remember that I learned the story from yesterday's interview.
entries.annotation_boundary: Distinguish forgotten origin from confident misattribution; neither necessarily makes the remembered content false.

entries.name: Spacing Effect
entries.operational_definition: Distributed study improves retention relative to massed study under comparable conditions.
entries.positive_example: With equal total practice, studying across four days produced better later recall than one continuous session.
entries.target_negative_example: The distributed group did better but also received twice as much practice.
entries.annotation_boundary: Compare spaced with massed practice; lag effect compares different gaps within spaced practice.

entries.name: Spotlight Effect
entries.operational_definition: Others' attention to one's appearance or behavior is overestimated.
entries.positive_example: I thought nearly everyone noticed the tiny stain, but the anonymous check showed almost nobody did.
entries.target_negative_example: Many people mentioned the stain, so I know they noticed it.
entries.annotation_boundary: Visibility of inner states is illusion of transparency; external attention is the key here.

entries.name: Status Quo Bias
entries.operational_definition: The existing or default option is favored simply because it is already in place.
entries.positive_example: The alternative is better on every criterion I care about and switching is effortless, but keep the current setting solely because it is current.
entries.target_negative_example: I keep the current service because switching would impose a substantial cost.
entries.annotation_boundary: Switching costs, uncertainty, or genuinely better fit can justify continuity.

entries.name: Suggestibility
entries.operational_definition: External suggestions influence beliefs, recollection, or behavior without adequate independent appraisal.
entries.positive_example: After the interviewer repeatedly suggested a red coat, I began recalling red even though my initial statement and the footage showed blue.
entries.target_negative_example: I updated the coat color after reviewing clear footage.
entries.annotation_boundary: Suggestion-based influence differs from evidence-based correction; memory effects can overlap source confusion.

entries.name: Survivorship Bias
entries.operational_definition: Visible survivors are analyzed while relevant missing failures are excluded.
entries.positive_example: Every business in our sample survived ten years, so its habits guarantee success; we never examined businesses that used the same habits and failed.
entries.target_negative_example: We compared surviving and failed businesses from the same starting cohort.
entries.annotation_boundary: Specify the selection process and omitted population; a sample of successes is not always inappropriate for a narrow descriptive question.

entries.name: Take-the-best Heuristic
entries.operational_definition: Options are selected using the first sufficiently discriminating cue in a prioritized cue order.
entries.positive_example: I compare battery life first; if it differs, I choose the longer-lasting device and stop without considering lower-ranked attributes.
entries.target_negative_example: I combine all relevant attributes using my predefined weighted score.
entries.annotation_boundary: A decision strategy that can be efficient; one decisive relevant criterion is not necessarily an error.

entries.name: Telescoping Effect
entries.operational_definition: Events are remembered as more recent or more distant than their actual dates.
entries.positive_example: I place the conference last spring, but dated records show it occurred four years ago.
entries.target_negative_example: I say I am unsure of the date and check my calendar.
entries.annotation_boundary: Forward telescoping brings old events closer; backward telescoping pushes recent events farther away.

entries.name: The Illusion of Explanatory Depth
entries.operational_definition: People overestimate how well they understand a mechanism until asked to explain it.
entries.positive_example: I said I understood the locking mechanism completely, but when asked for a step-by-step explanation I could not explain how its central parts interact.
entries.target_negative_example: I recognize the device but do not claim to understand its mechanism.
entries.annotation_boundary: Require an explanation-depth gap; general task overconfidence is broader.

entries.name: The Pygmalion effect
entries.operational_definition: Another person's high expectations change their treatment of someone and thereby improve that person's performance.
entries.positive_example: The coach expected progress, provided more constructive practice opportunities because of that expectation, and the player's performance improved.
entries.target_negative_example: The coach predicted improvement after seeing an already rising performance trend but changed no treatment.
entries.annotation_boundary: Require an expectation-to-treatment-to-performance pathway; a prediction alone is not a self-fulfilling effect.

entries.name: The Sunk Cost Fallacy
entries.operational_definition: Unrecoverable past expenditure is used to justify a choice despite unfavorable future costs and benefits.
entries.positive_example: Finishing will cost more than its remaining benefit, but we must continue because we already spent so much and cannot recover it.
entries.target_negative_example: We continue because the remaining benefit exceeds the remaining cost, regardless of past spending.
entries.annotation_boundary: Past costs are sunk only if unrecoverable; distinguish salvage value and future contractual consequences.

entries.name: Zero Risk Bias
entries.operational_definition: Eliminating one risk entirely is preferred over a larger overall risk reduction merely because it reaches zero.
entries.positive_example: With equal costs and harms, I prefer reducing a risk from 2% to 0% over reducing another from 20% to 10%, solely because zero feels safer.
entries.target_negative_example: I choose the larger reduction when costs and consequences are equivalent.
entries.annotation_boundary: Control harm severity, costs, and risk dependence; a zero endpoint is not automatically irrational.

entries.name: Duygu yüklü dil
entries.operational_definition: Değerlendirici sözcükler olayı olumlu veya olumsuz sunar.
entries.positive_example: Vatandaşın cebine yeni darbe.
entries.target_negative_example: Ücret 25 liradan 30 liraya yükseldi.
entries.annotation_boundary: Olumsuz olayın aktarılması tek başına yüklü dil değildir.

entries.name: Seçici istatistik
entries.operational_definition: Karşılaştırma tabanı veya payda seçimi sayının anlamını çarpıtır.
entries.positive_example: Başvuru iki katına çıktı; ancak 1 kişiden 2 kişiye çıktığı belirtilmedi.
entries.target_negative_example: Başvuru 1 kişiden 2 kişiye çıktı.
entries.annotation_boundary: Eksik paydanın mevcut ve ilgili olduğuna dair karşılaştırmalı kanıt gerekir.

entries.name: Tek taraflı kaynak seçimi
entries.operational_definition: İlgili karşı görüş mevcutken yalnızca bir tarafın iddiası haberin kanıtı olur.
entries.positive_example: Şirket açıklaması tek dayanak; aynı olay için işçi açıklaması da yayımlandı.
entries.target_negative_example: Şirket açıklamasına göre ücretler arttı; çalışanlar itiraz ediyor.
entries.annotation_boundary: Kısa RSS özeti bütün haberde karşı görüşün bulunmadığını kanıtlamaz.

entries.name: Vurgu çerçevelemesi
entries.operational_definition: Aynı olgunun farklı boyutları başlık ve sunumda öne çıkarılır.
entries.positive_example: Yeni tarife hizmeti iyileştirecek.
entries.target_negative_example: Yeni tarife ücret ve hizmet değişiklikleri içeriyor.
entries.annotation_boundary: Farklı vurgu tek başına yanlış bilgi veya kasıt değildir.

entries.name: Kanıtsız nedensellik
entries.operational_definition: Birlikte değişim veya zaman sırası tek başına neden olarak sunulur.
entries.positive_example: Başkan değişti, işsizlik düştü; demek ki düşüşü başkan sağladı.
entries.target_negative_example: Başkanın göreve başlamasından sonra işsizlik düştü; neden araştırılıyor.
entries.annotation_boundary: Açık nedensel ifade gerekir; sadece kronoloji yeterli değildir.

entries.name: Bağlam eksiltme
entries.operational_definition: Erişilebilir ve ilgili bağlamın dışarıda bırakılması karşılaştırmayı değiştirir.
entries.positive_example: Gelir arttı deniyor; aynı dönemde fiyatların daha hızlı arttığı verisi atlanıyor.
entries.target_negative_example: Gelir nominal arttı, fiyatlara göre azaldı.
entries.annotation_boundary: Omission Bias ile aynı değildir; tam metin ve ilgili karşı kanıt olmadan adaydır.
